concepts.title: Meaning and Functions of Political Parties

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Meaning and Functions of Political Parties' refers to.
questions.a: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government. They agree on some policies and programmes for society with a view to promoting the collective good.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meaning and Functions of Political Parties'.
questions.a: Political parties perform essential functions in a democracy: contesting elections, forming policies, forming and running governments, and linking citizens to the government.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meaning and Functions of Political Parties' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Why Do We Need Political Parties?

concepts.title: Party Systems: One-Party, Two-Party, and Multi-Party

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Party Systems: One-Party, Two-Party, and Multi-Party' refers to.
questions.a: A party system refers to the number and relative strength of political parties in a country. The main types are the one-party system, the two-party system, and the multi-party system.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Party Systems: One-Party, Two-Party, and Multi-Party'.
questions.a: The number of parties in a country depends on its social and regional diversity; no single system is ideal for all democracies.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Party Systems: One-Party, Two-Party, and Multi-Party' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: How Many Parties Should We Have?

concepts.title: National and Regional Parties in India

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'National and Regional Parties in India' refers to.
questions.a: National parties have presence in several states and are recognised by the Election Commission based on vote share and seats across the country. Regional parties (or state parties) have their base limited to a particular state or region.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'National and Regional Parties in India'.
questions.a: National parties address broad national issues while regional parties represent regional identities and interests; both are essential in India's federal democracy.

questions.q: Under which section is 'National and Regional Parties in India' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: National Parties

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Challenges to Political Parties' refers to.
questions.a: Political parties face several challenges in India: lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, growing role of money and muscle power, and lack of meaningful choice for voters due to ideological convergence.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Challenges to Political Parties'.
questions.a: The four major challenges -- lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, and absence of meaningful choice -- undermine the credibility and effectiveness of parties.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Challenges to Political Parties' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Challenges to Political Parties

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Party Reforms in India' refers to.
questions.a: Party reforms are measures to make political parties more democratic, transparent, and accountable. They include constitutional and legal changes, internal party regulations, and citizen-led efforts.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Party Reforms in India'.
questions.a: Reforms can be brought about through constitutional amendments, anti-defection laws, mandatory disclosure of assets, and public pressure, but require political will to be effective.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Party Reforms in India' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: How Can Parties Be Reformed?

concepts.title: Role of the Opposition in Democracy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Role of the Opposition in Democracy' refers to.
questions.a: The opposition consists of parties that are not part of the government. Its role is to criticise government policies, mobilise opposition, highlight failures, and provide alternative policies to the ruling party.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Role of the Opposition in Democracy'.
questions.a: A strong opposition is essential for accountability; it ensures that the government is responsive and that citizens have an alternative choice.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Role of the Opposition in Democracy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Functions of Political Parties

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Anti-Defection Law' refers to.
questions.a: The anti-defection law, passed in 1985, prevents elected members of a legislature from changing their party allegiance after election. If a member defects, they can lose their seat in the legislature.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Anti-Defection Law'.
questions.a: The anti-defection law was introduced to curb political horse-trading and ensure stability of governments by preventing legislators from switching parties for personal gain.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Anti-Defection Law' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Party Reforms

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Party Manifestos and Electoral Promises' refers to.
questions.a: A party manifesto is a document issued by a political party before elections that outlines its policies, programmes, and promises to voters if elected to power. It serves as a basis for voters to choose between parties.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Party Manifestos and Electoral Promises'.
questions.a: Manifestos provide voters with information about a party's priorities and serve as a benchmark for holding the party accountable after it comes to power.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Party Manifestos and Electoral Promises' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Functions of Political Parties

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Coalition Governments and Alliance Politics' refers to.
questions.a: A coalition government is formed when no single party wins a majority and two or more parties join together to form a government. Alliance politics refers to the pre-poll or post-poll partnerships among parties to contest or form governments.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Coalition Governments and Alliance Politics'.
questions.a: Coalition governments reflect the diversity of Indian society and ensure regional representation, but they can also lead to instability and compromise on policy clarity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Coalition Governments and Alliance Politics' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Party Systems
